posts.h1: How Do Permanent Christmas Lights Actually Work?
posts.title: How Permanent Christmas Lights Work — Plain English Guide
posts.desc: Plain-English explanation of how permanent Christmas lights work — the LED chip, the track, the controller, the app, and what that means for your home.
posts.kw: how do permanent christmas lights work
posts.lead: Most explanations sound like a brochure. Here's how the system actually works, what each piece does, and why it matters.

p: Each light is an RGBIC-RD LED — a small chip that can be told to be any of 16 million colors, individually. The 'IC' part means each LED has its own tiny driver, so the system can run a gradient or animation that flows pixel by pixel instead of one solid color across the whole house.

The LEDs sit inside a continuous aluminum channel that's screwed into the soffit substructure (same anchoring as your gutters). The track is color-matched to your trim — white, bronze, brown, or black — so by daylight you basically don't see it from the curb.
The aluminum part is rated for life. The LEDs themselves are rated 50,000+ hours, which works out to about 17 years at 8 hours a night.
A small weatherproof box mounted near your main electrical (usually inside the garage) sends data to every LED on the track. It connects to your home Wi-Fi and pairs with the app on your phone.
From the app you pick a scene (Christmas, Halloween, warm-white, game day) or schedule it. You can also tie it to Alexa, Google Home, Control4, or Nice Elan.
The whole assembly is rated IP67, which means dust-tight and submersible. Tested -40°F to 140°F. Engineered for the 115°F summer days and the rare Sierra winter — well outside Fresno's worst weather.

faqs.q: Do they use more electricity than regular Christmas lights?
faqs.a: Less. The whole system pulls about the same as a single 60W bulb when running a typical pattern. Run it 8 hours a night for a month, you're looking at a few dollars on the power bill.

faqs.q: What if the Wi-Fi goes out?
faqs.a: The control box stores its current schedule and keeps running. You just lose the ability to change scenes from the app until Wi-Fi is back.

posts.h1: How RGBIC LEDs Work (And Why It Matters Outside)
posts.title: How RGBIC LEDs Work | Permanent Outdoor Lighting Tech
posts.desc: How RGBIC LEDs work — per-pixel addressing, the IC chip, why pixel pitch matters, and why this beats RGB for permanent outdoor lighting.
posts.lead: If you've shopped permanent lighting, you've seen 'RGBIC' twenty times without anyone explaining it. Here's the actual mechanism.

p: Every visible color is mixed from red, green, and blue light at varying intensities. An RGB LED has three tiny sub-LEDs — one of each color — packed into a single housing. By varying the brightness of each, the LED produces 16 million color combinations.

The 'IC' is an integrated circuit — a tiny brain — built into each LED. It listens for instructions on a shared data line and lights up only when its address is called. So the controller can say 'pixel 47, turn purple at 60% brightness' and only that one LED responds.

Without the IC chip, every LED on the strip has to show the same color at the same time — that's plain RGB. With IC, each pixel runs independently, which is what enables flowing gradients, chase animations, and per-section color zones.

Outside is exactly where pixel-by-pixel control earns its money. Roofline outlines look static and cheap with single-color RGB. RGBIC produces the smooth color washes you see on display homes — twinkling Christmas reds-and-greens that actually fade into each other, fire-effect Halloween, USA flag waves on July 4.

faqs.q: Is RGBIC always better than RGB?
faqs.a: For outdoor permanent lighting, yes — by a lot. For a single accent strip behind a TV, plain RGB is fine and cheaper.
Marginally — the IC chips draw a tiny bit of standby power. Total draw is still negligible compared to incandescent Christmas lights.

posts.h1: How App-Controlled Outdoor Lights Actually Connect
posts.title: How App-Controlled Outdoor Lights Work | Wi-Fi & Smart Home
posts.desc: How permanent outdoor lights connect to your phone — the controller, the Wi-Fi, the cloud, and where each piece can break.
posts.kw: how app controlled outdoor lights work
posts.lead: Three components have to talk to each other for your phone to change a color. Here's the chain.

p: When you tap 'Christmas' in the app, your phone sends a message to the manufacturer's cloud server. The server pushes that command down to your control box over Wi-Fi. The box translates it into per-pixel commands for the LED strip.
It happens in well under a second on decent home Wi-Fi.

The control box stores its current scene and schedule on-device. If your Wi-Fi or the cloud goes down, lights keep running whatever they were last told to run. They just stop accepting new commands until connectivity returns.
Alexa and Google Home use a routine: you say 'Christmas mode' and Alexa sends an API call to the manufacturer's cloud, which forwards it to your box. Same chain, different starting point.
Control4 and Nice Elan integrations talk directly to the controller over your local network — no cloud round-trip — which is why they feel instant on professional smart-home setups.

faqs.a: The app sends scene names and schedules to the cloud — nothing identifying about your house or habits beyond that.

faqs.q: Will the system work if I switch ISPs?
faqs.a: Yes — just rejoin Wi-Fi from the app. Takes 60 seconds.

posts.title: Pixel Pitch in Permanent Outdoor Lighting | Plain English
posts.desc: Pixel pitch explained — the distance between LEDs, why it changes how patterns look, and what to ask before you buy.

p: Cheap consumer kits run roughly 6-inch pitch. Older pro systems are 4-5 inch. The Jellyfish RGBIC-RD that we install is roughly 4-inch pitch, which is at the high-density end for outdoor.

posts.h1: What Happens to Permanent Lights During a Power Outage?
posts.title: Permanent Lights & Power Outages | What to Expect
posts.desc: What happens to permanent outdoor lights during a blackout, what survives, what restarts, and whether anything gets damaged.
posts.lead: Short version: nothing dramatic. Lights go out, lights come back on. Here's the longer version.

p: No power, no lights. The control box and the LEDs all run on house current. If you've got a whole-home backup or solar with battery, the lights run on that just like any other circuit.

The control box reboots in about 20 seconds. It re-reads its stored schedule and resumes whatever scene was supposed to be running. If a Christmas pattern was on at 9pm and power comes back at 9:08, lights pick up at 9:08 like nothing happened.

Standard install includes a small surge protector inline with the controller. Big lightning hit can still kill electronics — that's what the 5-year LED warranty is for. We've replaced exactly two controllers in three years for surge damage, both covered.

posts.h1: What Does IP67 Actually Mean for Outdoor Lighting?
posts.title: IP67 Rating Explained for Permanent Outdoor Lights
posts.desc: What IP67 means in practical terms for permanent outdoor lighting — dust, rain, sprinklers, snow, and Fresno summer heat.
posts.lead: IP67 is a real test, not marketing copy. Here's what each digit means and why it matters in Fresno.

p: The first digit (6) rates dust ingress: 6 is the maximum — 'dust-tight,' nothing gets in. The second digit (7) rates water ingress: 7 means submersible to one meter for 30 minutes without leaking.
So an IP67 fixture can sit at the bottom of a kid's pool for half an hour and still light up. Sprinklers and rain aren't even close to a stress test.

Central Valley summers are dry and dusty — agricultural drift, the occasional Bakersfield haboob. Dust-tight matters more in Fresno than waterproof, honestly. Anything less than IP6X starts collecting silt internally and dimming over a few seasons.

UV rating, temperature range, and impact resistance are separate specs. The Jellyfish RGBIC-RD chips we install are also rated -40°F to 140°F and the aluminum track is anodized for UV — but IP67 alone doesn't tell you that. Always ask for the full spec.

p: A power supply that converts 120V house current down to 24V DC. A Wi-Fi radio. A microcontroller running the firmware. A surge protector. Terminal blocks for the data and power runs to the track.
All of it sits in a sealed weatherproof enclosure roughly 8x10x3 inches.

Almost always inside the garage on a wall close to the panel. Power source: a dedicated 15-amp circuit (we add the breaker if needed). Wi-Fi signal: needs decent reception — we test on install day before final mount.
If garage placement isn't possible, exterior mount on a north-facing wall works fine — IP67 enclosure handles it.
Nothing. It sits there for 17+ years. Firmware updates push automatically over Wi-Fi. The only time you touch it is if you change Wi-Fi networks (use the app).

faqs.a: Yes, but it's a 30-minute service call and the data run length needs to stay within spec. Plan placement once.

Cheap consumer kits use thermoplastics that go brittle around 120°F. We've replaced two Govee strips this summer for customers who switched after their DIY went soft.

posts.h1: Permanent Lights Won't Turn On: Step-by-Step Fix
posts.title: Permanent Lights Won't Turn On | Troubleshooting Steps
posts.desc: Step-by-step troubleshooting for permanent outdoor lighting that won't turn on — power, controller, app, schedule, support call.
posts.lead: 90% of 'lights won't turn on' calls are one of three things. Try these in order before calling.

p: Find the breaker labeled for the lighting controller (usually labeled at install). If it tripped, reset. Wait 30 seconds. Try the app.
If it trips again immediately, stop — likely a short. Call us.
Open the app. Look at the schedule for today. If you accidentally toggled 'off' or set the start time to a future date, you'll find it here. Most common cause.
Flip the lighting breaker off. Wait 30 seconds. Flip back on. Wait another 30 seconds for the controller to reconnect to Wi-Fi. Try the app.
Resolves about 80% of remaining issues.
Call us. Service calls under our 5-year workmanship warranty are free. Same-day in Fresno County.

posts.h1: Some LEDs Look a Different Color Than the Rest
posts.title: Permanent Lights Color Mismatch | Why It Happens, How to Fix
posts.desc: Why some LEDs in a permanent lighting strip look slightly different colors and what to do about it.
posts.lead: Almost always one of three causes. Here's how to diagnose without calling support first.

p: A few patterns intentionally have variable color across the strip — fire effect, gradient wash. If it only happens during specific scenes, that's by design.
Switch to solid white. If all LEDs match, it was the pattern.

body.h: Cause 2: Voltage drop on long runs
p: On runs over 50 ft, the LEDs at the far end can look slightly dimmer/yellower than the start. The control box adjusts for this with 'voltage compensation' — toggle it on in app settings if it's off.
If the issue persists, your installer may need to add a power injection point. Free service call under our workmanship warranty.
A single LED stuck on the wrong color is usually a hardware failure. Covered under the 5-year LED warranty. We'll replace the affected segment at no charge.

posts.h1: Permanent Lighting App Won't Connect: Fixes That Work

posts.desc: Step-by-step fixes when the permanent lighting app won't connect to your controller — Wi-Fi, router, app reset.

p: Sounds dumb. Solves a third of cases.

body.h: 2. Confirm phone and controller are on the same Wi-Fi network

Unplug for 30 seconds. Plug back in. Wait 90 seconds. Try the app. Solves another third.
Flip the lighting breaker off for 30 seconds, back on. Wait 60 seconds for Wi-Fi reconnect. Try the app.
In the app, remove the controller, then re-add as new device. Walks through Wi-Fi setup. Takes 3 minutes.

posts.h1: Permanent Lights Look Dim or Yellow-White: Fixes

The app has a master brightness slider. If it got bumped down to 30%, lights look dim. Slide back to 100%.
On long runs, the far end can look dim. Toggle 'voltage compensation' on in app settings. If still dim, schedule a free service call — we may need to add a power injection point.

posts.h1: Permanent Lights After a Power Surge: What to Check
posts.title: Permanent Lights After Power Surge | What to Check
posts.desc: What to check on permanent outdoor lighting after a power surge or lightning event, and what's covered under warranty.
posts.lead: Surge protector takes most hits. Sometimes the controller takes one. Here's how to tell.

p: Reset it. If everything comes back on, you're done.

body.h: Lights on but app won't connect
p: Wi-Fi radio in the controller may have taken a hit. Try a controller reboot. If still no connection, we replace the controller under warranty (5-year LED warranty covers controller too).
A section of LEDs likely failed. Affected segment replaced under warranty. We've replaced two segments in three years for surge damage — covered both times.

posts.h1: Cleaning Permanent Lights: Tree Sap, Dust, Spider Webs
posts.title: How to Clean Permanent Outdoor Lights | Maintenance Guide
posts.desc: How to clean permanent outdoor lighting safely — tree sap, Central Valley dust, spider webs, and what to never use.
posts.lead: Annual rinse keeps everything looking new. Anything more involved is rare.

p: Garden hose on a gentle setting, point up at the track from the ground. 30 seconds per side of the house. Knocks loose dust and any cobwebs.
Don't pressure-wash — IP67 handles it but the seal isn't designed for direct high-pressure jets.
Mix dish soap and warm water. Soft cloth on a paint-roller pole. Light wipe along the track. Rinse with hose.
Never use solvents (acetone, alcohol, paint thinner). They'll cloud the LED lenses permanently.

body.h: Heavy dust after a Valley dust storm
p: Same hose rinse, twice. If LEDs look hazy after, that's silica buildup on the lens — soft cloth wipe with the soapy-water mix removes it.

Volunteer to limit holiday schedule (ex: Christmas only Nov 25-Jan 6, Halloween only Oct 15-Nov 1). Some HOAs ask. Beat them to it.

posts.h1: Permanent Lights on Stucco vs Wood Fascia
posts.title: Permanent Lighting on Stucco vs Wood Fascia | Install Differences
posts.desc: How permanent outdoor lighting installs differ on stucco-only construction vs traditional wood fascia, and what to expect.
posts.lead: Wood fascia is the easy install. Stucco-only takes a different approach. Both work — costs differ.

p: Stainless screws into the wood substructure behind the soffit panels. Standard install. No special prep, no surface drilling.

No soffit, just a stucco eave. We use concealed brackets that anchor with smaller screws into the stucco lath structure (not just the surface stucco itself). Installer marks pilot points carefully — wrong screw placement crumbles stucco.
Adds about 10% to install time. Adds 5-8% to total cost. End result is identical from the curb.

Most common in Central Valley homes built 2000+. We work the wood eaves the standard way and skip the stucco walls entirely — track only goes where there's a structural anchor. Looks the same from the street.

posts.h1: Permanent Lights with Solar Panels: Compatible?
posts.title: Permanent Lights & Solar Panels | Compatibility Guide
posts.desc: How permanent outdoor lighting works with rooftop solar panels — install routing, electrical, and known issues.
posts.lead: Compatible. Common. Some routing details to know up front.

p: Track goes under the eave, panels go on top of the roof. Different planes, no physical conflict.

Lighting controller draws from the house panel like any other circuit. Solar feed-in doesn't affect it. Net-metering customers: lights run during sundown hours, when solar production is low — basically free electricity if you produce excess earlier in the day.
If you have whole-home backup (Tesla Powerwall, etc.), the lighting circuit is on it like everything else. Lights stay on through grid outages assuming battery isn't depleted.

posts.h1: Can You Move Permanent Lights to a New House?

posts.desc: Whether you can move permanent outdoor lighting to a new home, what's reusable, what's not, and the cost.
posts.lead: Short answer: rarely worth it. Long answer below.

p: The control box (basically). The app pairing. Maybe the LED strip if it's in good condition and the new house's geometry happens to match.
What's not reusable: the aluminum track. It's cut to fit the previous house's roofline and won't match the new one.
Removal from old house: ~$400. New install on new house with old hardware where possible: ~$1,800. Total: ~$2,200.
New install from scratch: $2,800. Difference: $600. Most clients pick new install — fewer compromises, full warranty resets.
You just installed within the last 12 months and the new house is structurally similar. Otherwise, sell the old install with the house and start fresh.

Screw holes the size of a finishing nail every 24 inches along the soffit substructure. One small hole where the data cable dropped to the attic. That's it.
If you pulled because of our 7-day refund, we patch the holes ourselves.
